title: Physical Quantities and Units
lead: Physics describes nature with numbers, and a number means little without a unit to say what it counts. This section defines a physical quantity, introduces the four fundamental units of the SI system and the metric prefixes that carry them across the immense range of lengths, masses, and times found in nature, and shows how a conversion factor changes a value from one unit to another.
objectives: Perform unit conversions both in the SI and English units.
Explain the most common prefixes in the SI units and be able to write them in scientific notation.
summary_html:
• Physical quantities are a characteristic or property of an object that can be measured or calculated from other measurements.
  • Units are standards for expressing and comparing the measurement of physical quantities. All units can be expressed as combinations of four fundamental units.
  • The four fundamental units we will use in this text are the meter (for length), the kilogram (for mass), the second (for time), and the ampere (for electric current). These units are part of the metric system, which uses powers of 10 to relate quantities over the vast ranges encountered in nature.
  • The four fundamental units are abbreviated as follows: meter, m; kilogram, kg; second, s; and ampere, A. The metric system also uses a standard set of prefixes to denote each order of magnitude greater than or lesser than the fundamental unit itself.
  • Unit conversions involve changing a value expressed in one type of unit to another type of unit. This is done by using conversion factors, which are ratios relating equal quantities of different units.

figures.original_caption: The meter is defined to be the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second in a vacuum. Distance traveled is speed multiplied by time.

exercises.prompt: Some hummingbirds beat their wings more than 50 times per second. A scientist is measuring the time it takes for a hummingbird to beat its wings once. Which fundamental unit should the scientist use to describe the measurement? Which factor of 10 is the scientist likely to use to describe the motion precisely? Identify the metric prefix that corresponds to this factor of 10.

answer.solution: The scientist will measure the time between each movement using the fundamental unit of seconds. Because the wings beat so fast, the scientist will probably need to measure in milliseconds, or $10^{-3}$ seconds. (50 beats per second corresponds to 20 milliseconds per beat.)

exercises.prompt: One cubic centimeter is equal to one milliliter. What does this tell you about the different units in the SI metric system?

answer.solution: The fundamental unit of length (meter) is probably used to create the derived unit of volume (liter). The measure of a milliliter is dependent on the measure of a centimeter.

exercises.prompt: Identify some advantages of metric units.

answer.solution: Conversions between metric units involve only powers of 10, since there are 100 centimeters in a meter and 1000 meters in a kilometer, whereas the relationships in U.S. customary units are not as simple, with 12 inches in a foot and 5280 feet in a mile. The same unit can be used over extremely large ranges of values simply by choosing an appropriate metric prefix, so meters serve in construction, kilometers in air travel, and nanometers in optical design, and there is no need to invent new units for particular applications. The metric system is also the standard agreed upon by scientists and mathematicians and used by virtually every country in the world, which makes measured values easy to express and compare.

exercises.prompt: The speed limit on some interstate highways is roughly 100 km/h. (a) What is this in meters per second? (b) How many miles per hour is this?

parts.hint: Two conversion factors are needed, one for kilometers to meters and one for hours to seconds, as in part (b) of Example 1.1.
A mile is about 1.61 km, so write the factor that cancels kilometers and leaves miles.

exercises.prompt: Show that $1.0\ \text{m/s} = 3.6\ \text{km/h}$. Hint: Show the explicit steps involved in converting $1.0\ \text{m/s} = 3.6\ \text{km/h}$.
Soccer fields vary in size. A large soccer field is 115 m long and 85 m wide. What are its dimensions in feet and inches? (Assume that 1 meter equals 3.281 feet.)

parts.hint: Multiply the length in meters by the factor that cancels meters and leaves feet.
There are 12 inches in 1 foot, so a second factor carries feet into inches.
The same factor of 3.281 feet per meter applies to the width.
Multiply the width in feet by 12 inches per foot.

exercises.prompt: Mount Everest, at 29,028 feet, is the tallest mountain on the Earth. What is its height in kilometers? (Assume that 1 kilometer equals 3,281 feet.)

answer.hint: Write the conversion factor with feet in the denominator so that feet cancel and kilometers remain.

exercises.prompt: Tectonic plates are large segments of the Earth’s crust that move slowly. Suppose that one such plate has an average speed of 4.0 cm/year. (a) What distance does it move in 1 s at this speed? (b) What is its speed in kilometers per million years?

parts.hint: Convert the speed to meters per second using the number of seconds in a year from Table 1.3, and the distance in 1 s is that speed times 1 s.
A million years is $10^{6}$ years and a kilometer is $10^{5}$ centimeters, so the two factors of 10 nearly cancel.
